title: Symphony No. 2 in E-flat major
hook: A symphony headed by Shelley’s “Spirit of Delight”, shadowed by the death of a king, and ending not in triumph but in a quiet glow.

painting.title: Interior of St. Mark’s, Venice
painting.pairingNote: The dim, gold-lit inside of St Mark’s, which Elgar saw in the spring of 1909; he said the step from the Larghetto to the Rondo was the step from this interior out into the sunlit square.

facts: Elgar had sketched ideas for a symphony in E-flat as early as 1903. A trip to Italy with his wife in the spring of 1909, above all a visit to Venice, set the plan going again. He sketched it during 1910 and wrote out the full score in two months of hard work early in 1911, finishing on 28 February. At the foot of the score he wrote two place names, “Venice” and “Tintagel”, the Cornish village where he had stayed in April 1910 at the summer home of his close friend Alice Stuart-Wortley.

The score is headed with two lines by Shelley: “Rarely, rarely, comest thou, / Spirit of Delight!” The “Spirit of Delight” is the leaping, then plunging [[motto|motto]] heard in the first bars; it comes back all through the symphony and once more at the very end.

King Edward VII died in May 1910, while Elgar was at work, and the symphony is dedicated to his memory. The slow movement sounds like a funeral march, but Elgar told his publisher it was conceived before the king’s death; friends he had lost, among them Alfred Rodewald in 1903, are also part of its story.

Elgar conducted the first performance on 24 May 1911 at the Queen’s Hall in London. The hall was not full and the applause was polite rather than warm; afterwards he told the violinist W. H. Reed that the audience sat there “like a lot of stuffed pigs”. The symphony took years to find its public, helped by Adrian Boult, whose performance in 1920 made Elgar say his reputation was safe in his hands.
bigPicture.inOneLine: energy and a ghostly night (I), a funeral march (II), the bright square outside and a fever that breaks in on it (III), and a long, calm close in which the Spirit of Delight returns (IV).

movements.heading: Allegro vivace e nobilmente
movements.summary: The longest movement, and the busiest: a crowd of short themes, one after another, in a rhythm that swings in groups of three. In the middle the energy drains away and something stranger takes over, which Elgar described as a love scene in a garden at night “when the ghost of some memories comes through it”.

mainIdeas.name: The Spirit of Delight
mainIdeas.description: a wide leap upwards, then a plunge, in strings and high woodwind, the motto of the whole symphony.

mainIdeas.name: The quiet theme
mainIdeas.description: a soft, wistful violin melody, which Elgar wanted played very quietly but with full expression.

mainIdeas.name: The cello song
mainIdeas.description: a long, slow, singing line, tinged with nostalgia.

stops.hear: The whole orchestra springs up with a leap and a fall, and theme follows theme without a pause
stops.happening: The Spirit of Delight, then the first group of themes

stops.hear: The music slows and quietens; the violins sing a gentle tune, horns answering softly
The cellos take a long, slow, singing melody
stops.happening: A song-like theme, still within the [[exposition|exposition]]

stops.hear: The pace picks up again and a trumpet call bursts through a heroic, swaggering passage
The music turns shadowy and unsettled, with sliding scales
A hushed, dreamy stretch; a soft, insistent throbbing creeps in underneath, grows, fades and returns
stops.happening: The “ghost” passage Elgar said made him shiver

stops.hear: Trombones and tuba begin a soft march that swells to full strength
The opening themes return, with all their first energy

stops.label: Last 2 minutes
stops.hear: A brief calm, then the motto blazes out once more and the movement ends in a rush

notice: Listen for the falling shape of the motto in the first seconds. Once you know it, you will hear it in every movement, slowed down, darkened or broken up.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Daniel Barenboim recorded the symphony with the London Philharmonic Orchestra for CBS in the 1970s; this second recording, with the Staatskapelle Berlin, was made in the Berlin Philharmonie in October 2013. As a young man Barenboim worked often with John Barbirolli, one of the great Elgar conductors. Most recordings of the symphony have been made by British orchestras; here a German orchestra brings a dark, rich string sound to it.

movements.heading: Larghetto
movements.summary: A slow march in C minor, with the tread of a funeral procession. Elgar connected its opening with the interior of St Mark’s in Venice. Two great climaxes rise out of it, and when the march returns an oboe sings a free lament above it.

mainIdeas.name: The march
mainIdeas.description: a grave melody in winds and brass over soft chords throbbing on the second and fourth beats.

mainIdeas.name: The sigh
mainIdeas.description: a short, falling figure in the woodwind.

mainIdeas.name: The second theme
mainIdeas.description: a hushed, lyrical melody in the strings, which later grows into a climax marked *[[nobilmente|nobilmente]]*, “nobly”.

stops.hear: Soft, slow string chords, as if in a large, dim space
Muffled drum taps and pulsing chords; a solemn melody in the winds and brass
The woodwinds sigh in short falling phrases
stops.happening: A link to the second theme

stops.hear: The strings take over, quietly and tenderly
stops.happening: The second theme, in F minor

stops.hear: The music quickens and swells into a great major-key outburst in the brass
stops.happening: The first climax, marked *nobilmente e semplice*

stops.hear: The march comes back; above it a solo oboe sings a slow, free, keening line
stops.happening: The return, with the oboe’s lament

stops.hear: A slow climb, half-step by half-step, rises to the loudest moment of the movement

stops.label: Last 90 seconds
stops.hear: The music sinks; a sudden swell in trombones and strings is cut off, and the end is almost silent

notice: At the oboe’s lament Elgar told the orchestra to imagine “a great crowd of silent people” watching a beloved sovereign pass, and the oboist to play freely: “It must sound as if it belonged outside somewhere”. Listen to how loosely the oboe line floats over the strict march beneath it.

movements.heading: Rondo. Presto
movements.summary: Out of the church into the sunlit square: Elgar said the main theme came from the “broken accent” of a tune played by street musicians in the Piazza San Marco. The [[rondo|rondo]] theme keeps coming back between other episodes, until a nightmare of hammering drums breaks in.

mainIdeas.name: The rondo theme
mainIdeas.description: quick, light and jerky, tossed between strings and woodwind.

mainIdeas.name: The sweeping theme
mainIdeas.description: a loud, rushing minor-key melody in the strings.

mainIdeas.name: The hammering
mainIdeas.description: a beat pounded out by drums, brass and tambourine that swamps everything.

stops.hear: A quick, skittering tune, passed back and forth between strings and woodwind
The strings sweep in loudly in the minor, with accents in brass and drums
The skittering tune again, now in earnest
Gentle woodwind melodies, like a pastoral scene; softly in the background the timpani tap a repeated beat
stops.happening: A calm episode, with a warning underneath

stops.hear: The tapping grows into a relentless pounding in drums, brass and tambourine; the ghostly figure from the first movement returns
stops.happening: The climax: “the madness that attends the excess or abuse of passion”, Elgar said

stops.hear: The storm fades as if nothing had happened; the earlier themes return

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: A final rush and a hard, triumphant chord in C major

notice: Elgar linked the pounding to lines in Tennyson’s *Maud*, where a man imagines himself dead and buried and hears “the hoofs of the horses beat, beat into my scalp and brain”. Notice how the beat starts quietly, long before it takes over.

movements.heading: Moderato e maestoso
movements.summary: A broad, steady finale in which, as Elgar wrote to his publisher, the sorrow of the earlier movements is “smoothed out and ennobled”. It ends quietly, with the Spirit of Delight returning slowly, like a sunset.

mainIdeas.name: The walking theme
mainIdeas.description: a calm, swaying melody in the cellos and low woodwind, every bar in the same rhythm.

mainIdeas.name: “Hans himself”
mainIdeas.description: a broad *nobilmente* theme, which Elgar linked with the conductor Hans Richter, his friend and champion.

mainIdeas.name: The motto
mainIdeas.description: the Spirit of Delight, back at the end, now slow and soft.

stops.hear: A calm, swaying melody in the low strings and woodwind, then repeated with a new line above
Sharper, more forceful music builds to a grand climax
A broad, noble melody, rising and falling
Instruments enter one after another on a busy idea, overlapping in a dense weave
Brass and drums hammer out the main theme, and a trumpet holds a piercing high note above the whole orchestra
The swaying main theme again, back in the home key
The music grows calmer; the cellos sing the main theme, then the woodwinds bring back the Spirit of Delight, slowly

stops.label: Last 2 minutes
stops.hear: High strings and soft brass fade into a warm, quiet close

notice: The trumpet’s high note at the climax is written to last one bar. At one performance the trumpeter Ernest Hall held it for two; Elgar was delighted, and many trumpeters have held it longer ever since.

threads.title: The Spirit of Delight
threads.body: The motto that opens the symphony returns in every movement in some form, from the ghost passage of the first to the slow, glowing reprise at the very end.

threads.title: Venice and Tintagel
threads.body: The two places written on the score: the dark church and the bright square of Venice in the middle movements, and Tintagel, which has not been tied to any one passage.

threads.title: A quiet ending
threads.body: Elgar’s First Symphony ended in triumph; this one fades away. That may be one reason the first audience was cool, and why later listeners have come to treasure it.
